findings.title: Blocked email lookup is case/format sensitive and easily bypassed
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) does a plain `where(email: email)` match with no normalization (no downcasing, no stripping). Users can trivially bypass the block by registering with different casing (e.g. 'Bad@SpamClub.com' vs a stored 'bad@spamclub.com') or surrounding whitespace. The User model stores emails without downcasing (only some flows use Email.downcase), so a blocked address will still validate successfully whenever the submitted string isn't byte-identical to the stored one. The lookup and the stored records should be normalized (downcase/strip, ideally at both write time in a before_validation on BlockedEmail and at lookup time).

findings.title: Validation has write side effects: should_block? saves records during model validation
findings.body: EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which increments match_count and saves the record. This means every User validation run (including intermediate validations, invalid attempts, or any other code path that calls user.valid?) performs a database write. Consequences: side effects from a read-only operation, writes inside validation callbacks, and skewed match_count statistics from repeated failed signup attempts. The statistic update should be decoupled from the predicate (e.g. done only on actual signup attempts in the controller, or via an atomic UPDATE).

findings.title: match_count increment is a read-modify-write race
findings.body: should_block? increments match_count in Ruby (`record.match_count += 1`) and saves the full record. Under concurrent signup attempts for the same email, increments can be lost, and full-record saves can also overwrite other columns with stale values. Use an atomic counter update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])`.

findings.title: Blocked-email check only runs when email_changed?, skipping existing users
findings.body: The `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` guard means the BlockedEmail check is skipped for any record whose email attribute was not changed (e.g. a previously-created user whose email was later added to the block list, or records loaded and re-saved). If the intent is only to gate signups this is fine, but the BlockedEmail feature then provides no protection on any path where an existing/loaded user is validated or saved (e.g. password_reset saves the user with the same email). Confirm the guard matches the intended scope of the blocklist.
